title: Two cortical mechanisms for natural audiovisual processing
abstract: Understanding how the human brain processes natural audiovisual information remains a central challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Progress has been limited by the difficulty of modeling complex audiovisual stimuli; prior work has therefore relied largely on short, controlled, or unimodal stimuli, leaving cortical mechanisms supporting real-world comprehension poorly characterized. Although recent AI advances enable extraction of high-dimensional, time-resolved features from naturalistic stimuli, how cortical regions dynamically prioritize auditory and visual information as time unfolds remains largely unexplored. Using large-scale fMRI data collected during movie viewing, we developed two complementary prediction-based approaches to map moment-by-moment sensory processing across cortex: one detects sustained periods when one modality predicts a region better than the other, identifying regions that switch the modality they encode for meaningful stretches of time; while the other identifies periods when both modalities predict the region well, revealing balanced audiovisual representations. Together, these analyses reveal two cortical patterns of audiovisual processing: two modality-switching ``bows" (a posterior bow encircling category-selective visual cortex and an anterior bow spanning dorsolateral frontal cortex) and an arrow-like axis jointly representing both modalities (extending from lateral occipital into temporal cortex). We further show that switching is not driven by reduced low-level information in the non-dominant modality, but by reduced cortical encoding of that information, suggesting active sensory reweighting. Modality dominance also cannot be explained simply by the dominant modality conveying a region's preferred concepts; switching regions do not merely track whichever modality expresses these concepts.Together, these systems suggest a cortical architecture that adaptively reweights sensory inputs while maintaining balanced multimodal representations during naturalistic comprehension.

title: Direct CDK1 engagement underlies carbaryl-induced genotoxic cell cycle arrest
authors: Piyush, R.; Tayade, S.; Shinde, S. R.
abstract: Carbaryl, a widely used carbamate pesticide, has been epidemiologically associated with genotoxic and carcinogenic outcomes in exposed human populations, including elevated cancer risk at several tissue sites and, in some agricultural communities, chronic tubulointerstitial kidney disease of unknown etiology (CKDu). However, the cellular mechanisms underlying these associations, and whether carbaryl acts uniformly across tissues, remain poorly defined. Screening a panel of cell lines of distinct species and lineage, we found that carbaryl elicits pronounced, dose-dependent cytotoxicity and cell cycle arrest selectively in a renal tubular epithelial line (IMCD3) and, to a lesser extent, a cervical epithelial line (HeLa), while a fibroblast line (NIH3T3) was unaffected. In IMCD3 cells, carbaryl induces S- and G2/M-phase arrest through direct binding to DNA and consequent DNA damage, triggers Bcl-2-mediated late apoptosis independently of reactive oxygen species, and drives irreversible mitotic arrest. Molecular dynamics simulations, cellular thermal shift assays, and kinase measurements converge on CDK1 as a direct target of carbaryl: carbaryl destabilises the CDK1 active site and inhibits its catalytic activity, whereas CDK2 is engaged through an opposing, rigidifying mode with no functional consequence. This asymmetry provides a coherent mechanistic basis for the combined S-phase and G2/M arrest observed. Together, these findings establish carbaryl as a genotoxic, cell-cycle-disrupting agent with tissue-selective potency acting directly on CDK1, and provide a cell-based mechanistic framework for interpreting its reported associations with renal and other tissue pathologies in exposed human populations.

title: Initiation codon context governs translation-coupled mRNA decay and coordinated expression in the human parasite Leishmania
authors: SANTI, A. M. M.; COKELAER, T.; PIPOLI DA FONSECA, J.; JENKINS, P.; TIKHONOVA, E. B.; RODRIGUEZ-ALMONACID, C.; KARAMYSHEV, A.; KARAMYSHEVA, Z.; SPÄTH, G.
abstract: In the absence of canonical, promoter-based transcriptional regulation, Leishmania has evolved alternative regulatory mechanisms for adaptive gene expression, including post-transcriptional control via differential mRNA turnover. While this mechanism is recognized as critical in Leishmania, fundamental aspects of transcript stability in these parasites remain to be elucidated, such as the role of translation initiation-mediated mRNA decay. We addressed this important gap by investigating the role of the initiation codon context (Kozak sequence) in gene expression in L. donovani. Mapping Kozak sequences across the trypanosomatid genomes revealed important differences in nucleotide preference across the genus and sub-genus levels, suggesting important cis-regulatory function. Within a single species, only a small subset of possible Kozak sequences is associated with several start codons, further supporting their role in expression control. Transgenic L. donovani lines expressing EGFP under the control of distinct Kozak variants indeed demonstrated that the nucleotide context of the start codon directly modulates both protein expression and mRNA stability, which was associated with increased recruitment of mRNA to heavy polysomes. Parasite exposure to the translation inhibitor cycloheximide restored EGFP expression driven by a weak Kozak sequence, revealing a direct link between mRNA stability and Kozak-mediated translatability. RNA-seq analysis of parasites arrested for transcription or translation elongation revealed transcripts enriched for the GO terms RNA modification and pseudouridine synthesis as key targets for translation-dependent mRNA turnover. The segregation of these transcripts into functional clusters with distinct Kozak profiles further suggests that Kozak sequence composition defines Kozak-governed regulons in Leishmania. Within this regulatory framework, the -3 nucleotide is identified as the key positional determinant driving differential transcript abundance. Our work uncovers a key role for translation initiation-coupled mRNA decay in Leishmania gene expression regulation adding a previously underappreciated layer of post-transcriptional regulation in parasite adaptation.

title: A Large Yield Model for Crop Production and Design in Western Canada
authors: Ubbens, J.; Loliencar, P.; Kagale, S.
abstract: With a changing climate, disease pressure, and other production threats, it is critical to ensure that crop producers are well-positioned to protect and optimize yields. In this work we present LYM-1, the first large-scale, multi-crop model for the prediction of yield performance in the Canadian prairies. This is enabled by a large dataset containing over 4.7 million yield observations across 10 different crop types, distributed over 23 growing years. Leveraging additional data sources for weather and soil properties allows the model to reason about the complex interactions between genetics, environment, and management which underlie yield. The trained model is not only effective at predicting the yield for held-out data, but also reveals scientifically and agronomically relevant effects such as the interaction between solar radiation and nitrogen uptake. We show that the architecture and training approach used in LYM-1 allows it to perform inference given incomplete queries where some model inputs are unspecified, while also establishing an advantage over popular linear and machine learning models in predictive performance.

title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism
authors: Naples, A. J.; Cayir, S.; cukar-capizzi, C.; Wolf, J. M.; Mcclelland, J. E.; Robertson, E. C.; Sawant, S. S.; Matuskey, D.; McPartland, J.
abstract: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [11C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.

title: Thalamic Dysconnectivity and Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder
authors: Kunitoki, K.; Adhikari, B. M.; Ankeeta, A.; Gao, S.; Ma, Y.; Straub, K. T.; Dos Santos Alves Maria, G.; Pagan, A. F.; Warner, A. R.; Du, X.; Kochunov, P.; Hong, L. E.
abstract: Background and Hypothesis Negative symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) are associated with poor functional outcomes and reduced quality of life; however, effective treatments remain limited. A better understanding of the underlying brain mechanisms is needed to develop better treatments. Neuroimaging studies implicate multiple brain networks in negative symptoms, though findings remain heterogeneous, potentially reflecting the multidimensionality of both symptoms and brain networks. Larger, more systematic dissections are required to identify the key hub(s) underlying negative symptoms. Study Design Structural MRI data from 394 participants (210 SSD, 184 healthy controls [HC]) were analyzed to identify cortical thickness and subcortical volume demonstrating both SSD-HC differences and associations with negative symptoms measured by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS). Regions meeting both criteria were selected as seeds for resting-state functional connectivity analyses in 143 SSD patients to examine association with negative symptoms and their subdomains. Study Results The thalamus was the only region demonstrating significant structural abnormalities both in SSD and an association with BNSS total score (p-FDR<0.05). Functional-network-defined thalamic subregions were subsequently examined. Several thalamic hypoconnectivities were significantly corresponded with negative symptoms, involving thalamic subregions associated with the cortical default mode, somatosensory, medial temporal, and dorsal attention networks (p=0.001, corrected<0.05). Blunted affect showed the most extensive thalamic connectivity alterations, involving the striatum, cerebellum, and temporoparietal junction/superior temporal sulcus (TPJ-STS). Thalamic hypoconnectivity with TPJ-STS was also associated with overall negative symptoms and anhedonia. Conclusions This study identifies the thalamus as a central hub of negative symptom-related dysfunction in SSD and highlights specific thalamic subnetworks as potential targets for circuit-based interventions.

title: Clustered and diffuse sensory corticostriatal wirings define complementary interneuron circuits
authors: Contadini, J.; Fino, E.; Bureau, I.
abstract: In the striatum, interneurons tightly control the activity of output neurons, the striatal projection neurons (SPN). Among these striatal interneurons, parvalbumin-expressing (PV) and somatostatin-expressing (SOM) cells exhibit markedly distinct electrophysiological and anatomical properties, suggesting differential integration into striatal circuits and distinct forms of feedforward inhibition onto SPN. However, it remains unclear whether differences already emerge at the level of corticostriatal connectivity and if they shape specific interactions with cortical inputs to SPN. Here, we investigated the spatial organization of the projections from the primary and secondary somatosensory areas (S1 and S2), onto striatal PV and SOM interneurons and SPN. With a combination of anatomical tracing and functional circuit mapping, we characterized key features of corticostriatal connectivity, including input number, origin, spacing, overlap and strength. We found that input spacing and strength, at both the individual cell and population levels, were the principal features distinguishing PV and SOM interneurons. In contrast, connectivity differed primarily in input number and laminar organization across S1 and S2. Our findings suggest two potential modes of interaction between interneurons and SPN connectivity: one in which PV interneurons receive S1 inputs structured in large clusters, that densely overlap with those of neighboring SPN, providing an anatomical substrate for potential neuronal assemblies. And another in which SOM interneurons also receive abundant cortical inputs, but thinly disseminated across S1 and S2 and that overlap little with those of SPN, potentially shaping these cell integration through input cross-interaction. These cell-type principles of corticostriatal wiring may support distinct forms of striatal computation.

title: Learning source weights for target-position estimation: comparing fixed weights and an input-dependent rule
abstract: Estimating an object's location requires combining uncertain measurements. Weights derived from an earlier calibration may become inappropriate when measurement errors change. We examined whether learning from noisy reference measurements improves position estimates, and whether weights computed from current inputs improve further than one learned set of weights used throughout evaluation. In simulations, we generated noisy position measurements of a target that remained fixed within each trial. Each two-input method combined the current measurement with the mean of three initial measurements. Measurement-accuracy reductions and added measurement offsets applied only after initialization. The estimator received no current or previous true target position. We repeated coordinate calibration, training, validation, and independent evaluation 100 times in each of four error conditions. Recalibration and fixed-weight learning explained most of the improvement over earlier supplied weights under reduced measurement accuracy and temporal correlation. With occasional large measurement errors, input-dependent weighting reduced mean squared error by 4.05% relative to learned fixed weights and assigned lower mean weights to measurements with added offsets. Its additional benefit was below 0.5% under independent errors and reduced current accuracy, while fixed weights had slightly lower mean error under temporal correlation. Methods using longer observation histories performed better in several conditions. Sensitivity analysis showed that shared coordinate bias and correlated reference errors limit conclusions about physical accuracy. The results show benefits and limits of recalibration, input-dependent weighting, and observation history within these measurement models.

title: Lactate epigenetically shapes tumor cell states in H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas
authors: Lum, J.; Nuechterlein, N.; Sliger, S.; Eyunni, S.; Tamrazi, B.; Bluml, S.; Tian, W.; Deogharkar, A.; Sweha, S. R.; Mota, M.; Bayliss, J.; Peterson, E.; Ji, S.; Wittwer, M.; Bhat, K.; Mott, B. T.; Hamanishi, E. T.; Merkuri, F.; Azambuja, A.; Conceicao, H.; Su, F.; Cao, X.; Pandey, R.; Ljare, O. B.; Parolia, A.; Yadav, V. N.; Wahl, D. R.; Koschmann, C.; Simoes-Costa, M.; Pichumani, K.; Wang, S.; Chinnaiyan, A. M.; Venneti, S.
abstract: H3K27M diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are lethal and lack treatment options. These tumors exhibit tumor heterogeneity with aggressive oligodendrocyte precursor (OPC)- and mesenchymal (MES)-like cell states. Because all tumor cells bear H3K27M, tumor heterogeneity has been attributed to microenvironmental cues that remain obscure. H3K27M DMGs exhibit increased glycolysis and the Warburg effect to produce lactate. Lactate can directly modify histone lysines including H3K27Lac, and we hypothesized that lactate epigenetically regulates tumor cell states in H3K27M DMGs. We undertook a comprehensive and integrated analysis of H3K27M DMG cell lines, animal models, tumor tissues, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy in patients to decipher the epigenetic roles of lactate. Here, we report that H3K27M cells uniquely exhibit elevation of the activating mark H3K27Lac. We observed significant heterogeneity in lactate levels within tumors, and the addition of exogenous lactate resulted in marked increases in H3K27Lac and the expression of critical OPC- and MES- like gene signature genes, which correlates with poorer patient outcomes. Our therapeutic approach leverages the inhibition of CBP/p300, which deposits both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac. Targeting CBP/p300 effectively reduces both H3K27Lac and H3K27ac levels, suppresses key OPC- and MES-like signatures, and shows efficacy in preclinical models. Collectively, our findings identify lactate as a key player in the epigenetic regulation of tumor cell state heterogeneity and suggest that targeting this pathway offers promise for addressing the heterogeneous complexities of H3K27M DMGs.

title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
authors: Du, Y.; Lin, A.; Brown, J. A. R.; Howe, L.; Xao, W.
abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

title: Metatranscriptomic Identification of Co- and Incidental Infections in Marine Turtles Reveals Complex Disease Aetiologies
authors: Lim, L.; Lang, B.; Fenton, H.; Rose, K. C.; Hall, J.; Holmes, E. C.
abstract: Traditional veterinary pathology investigations on wild animals generally conclude a primary cause of death based on a combination of observed clinical signs, gross and microscopic lesions, microbial culture and PCR. However, these methods may fail to capture the broader microbial community of the host. We employed metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the potential pathobiome of necropsied marine turtles, comparing these findings with corresponding veterinary pathology reports. Tissue samples were collected from 76 individuals spanning three species of marine turtles -- the green turtle (Chelonia mydas), the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), and the loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) -- across the coastline of New South Wales, Australia. Reported causes of mortality ranged from infectious disease to trauma. We identified a diverse range of parasites within the genera Neospirochis, Hapalotrema, Paraorgymatobothrium, Eimeria and Callitetrarhynchus, and bacteria including the genera Aeromonas, Clostridium, and Vibrio. Novel viruses of the families Astroviridae, Caliciviridae, Hepaciviridae, Hepeviridae, Nyamivirdae, Orthomyxoviridae, Picobirnaviridae and Rhabdoviridae were also identified. In cases where infectious disease was noted in the pathology report, we frequently observed high pathogen read counts consistent with the listed primary diagnoses. However, we also detected a range of incidental infections involving eukaryotic parasites, bacteria, and viruses. The diversity of infectious agents detected in marine turtles suggests that the observed disease outcomes are unlikely to be driven by a single causative agent, but rather by complex interactions between host health, the pathobiome, and environmental stressors. We discuss the potential implications for turtle health and conservation.

title: Patronin condensation integrates recognition, protection and organization of microtubule minus ends
authors: Zhang, B.; Yang, J.; Yu, S.; Zhou, K.; He, L.; Huang, L.; Liang, X.; Wang, H.; Chen, J.
abstract: Microtubule minus ends are central to non-centrosomal microtubule organization, yet how their recognition, protection and molecular organization are integrated remains unclear. Here we show that Drosophila Patronin forms dynamic condensates at microtubule minus ends through a prion-like domain (PrLD). PrLD-mediated condensation cooperates with the CKK domain and a second CKK-independent recognition region to convert weak or broadly distributed microtubule-binding activities into persistent minus-end recognition and tracking. Replacing the PrLD with a heterologous phase-separating HNRNPA1 IDR restores minus-end targeting, indicating that condensation capacity rather than PrLD primary sequence is critical. Patronin condensates further form a protective cap that resists minus-end depolymerization and recruit the cytoskeletal regulators Sas-4, Katanin and Ena. Disrupting PrLD multivalency impairs Patronin localization at multiple developmental sites and causes early organismal lethality. Thus, Patronin condensation creates a physiologically essential microtubule minus-end compartment coupling end recognition, stabilization and cytoskeletal organization.

title: A dsRNA Virus Converts Early Endosomes into Stable Replication Organelles Through Maturation Arrest and Retrograde Transport
authors: Gimenez, M. C.; Ferrero, D.; Issa, M.; Moussaoui, S.; Cabrini, M.; Reboucas Paixao, A.; Liu, L.; Ganesan, S.; Acharya, D.; Boermel, M.; Zaremberg, V.; Verdaguer, N.; Terebiznik, M.
abstract: Infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) and infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) are major animal pathogens that impose a heavy burden on the poultry and aquaculture industries. Yet, major aspects of their unique replication program remain unknown. IBDV is unusual among double-stranded RNA viruses in that it replicates in association with host endosomes. We previously demonstrated this association to be orchestrated by the viral protein VP3 and the early endosomal lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PtdIns(3)P], suggesting an essential role for VP3 in forming birnaviruses specialized replication compartments. Here, combining high-resolution fluorescence and correlative light-electron microscopy with diverse molecular and biochemical analyses, we define how the IBDV protein VP3 targets and remodels host endosomes, and establish that endosome-associated replication is conserved in members of the Birnaviridae family. We show that IBDV VP3 targets early endosomes via the PtdIns(3)P effector Early Endosomal Antigen 1 (EEA1) to arrest their maturation and prompt their association with the Golgi complex via ESCPE-1-mediated retrograde transport. We further show that IPNV also exploits endosomal membranes for replication in a PtdIns(3)P dependent manner, although for this virus VP3 engages endosomes through an EEA1-independent mechanism yet to be determined. This work uncovers how birnaviruses exploit a single viral protein to orchestrate endosome remodeling and intracellular trafficking to establish specialized replication compartments while revealing both conserved and host-adapted features of birnaviruses replication.

title: ESX-1 remodels the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen storage compartment in macrophages
authors: Luk, C. H.; Auchynnikava, T.; Fearns, A.; Ortiz Canseco, J.; Lockwood, P. K.; Charoy, C.; Gutierrez, M. G.
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) secretes antigenic proteins that drive protective T cell responses, yet how Mtb intracellular localization affects the trafficking and spatiotemporal distribution of mycobacterial antigens in macrophages remains elusive. Here, we developed a split fluorescent protein reporter to monitor the dynamics of the TB vaccine lead antigen Ag85B in infected human macrophages. We discovered that Mtb triggers the formation and remodeling of two distinct types of Mtb Antigen Storage Compartment (MASC) that retains Ag85 within macrophage membranes. Using subcellular spatial proteomics, we profiled the composition of the MASC, identifying both the Mtb and macrophage proteins that constitute these compartments. Unexpectedly, MASCs are defined by metabolic compartmentalization and rewiring to lipid metabolism in both the macrophage and Mtb. Thus, Mtb builds via the ESX-1 system a metabolically distinct antigen storage compartment in immune cells, with potential implications for antigen selection and delivery in TB vaccine development.

title: Ambient-Condition Visualization of Metalloenzyme Reactive Intermediates Enabled by the SHINERS Paradigm
authors: Liao, L.; Li, Q.-Q.; Zhang, X.; Liu, J.; Chen, Z.-H.; Zhou, Y.; Bao, Z.; Ma, H.; Yang, L.; Wang, X.; Wang, C.; Ren, B.; Li, J.-F.; Wang, B.
abstract: Reactive metal-oxygen intermediates are central to metalloenzyme catalysis, yet their low populations and short lifetimes make vibrational characterization under aqueous reaction conditions challenging. Here, we establish shell-isolated nanoparticle-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SHINERS) as a powerful vibrational approach for visualizing reaction-associated metal-ligand signatures of reactive metalloenzyme states. Across the heme and non-heme iron enzymes TauD, VioC, CYP119, and TqaLNc, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational information on reactive coordination states. In TauD and VioC, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational characterization of Fe(IV)=O intermediates. In CYP119, an isotope-sensitive Fe(IV)=O vibration is assigned to P450 Compound I generated by m-CPBA, including under lauric-acid turnover conditions. Most notably, in TqaLNc, combined 18O- and 15N-sensitive vibrational responses support formation of the proposed (R)HN-Fe(IV)=O coordination state and the dynamic-coordination mechanism underlying selective C-N bond formation. These results demonstrate that SHINERS can serve as a powerful technique for the in situ vibrational visualization of reactive intermediates and their coordination states in metalloenzyme catalysis.

title: Circular Data Analysis for Spatial Omics
authors: Shin, J.; Yoo, J.; Cho, Y.; Gupta, A.; Mao, P.-H.; Thakkar, K.; Eddy, T. A.; Chung, K. J.; Kim, J.; Jeon, H.; Xie, J.; Chung, D.
abstract: Many biological quantities in omics are inherently periodic or directional, including circadian phase, cell-cycle position, and cellular orientation. Treating such quantities as ordinary linear variables can introduce artificial discontinuities and obscure biological interpretation. Circular methods are well developed across directional statistics, bioinformatics, and spatial statistics, but practical guidance for omics applications remains limited. We present key considerations for circular data analysis in single-cell and spatial omics, including the provenance and observational unit of the circular quantity, the inferential or predictive objective, the distinction between tissue composition and residual spatial dependence, and the choice of appropriate models. We describe relevant approaches for circular representation, inference, clustering, regression, machine learning, and spatial analysis, together with representative R software. Their practical use is illustrated through spatial transcriptomic case studies of derived circadian peak phase in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease and latent cell-cycle position in human ovarian cancer. These examples demonstrate how the definition of the angle, its observational unit, and tissue heterogeneity shape appropriate analysis and interpretation, including when spatial modeling is not warranted. We conclude with practical recommendations and directions for future methodological development.

title: Complex folding kinetics of multi-domain proteins disentangled with periodic forces by magnetic tweezers
authors: Quintana-Catano, C. A.; Hartmann, A.; Schlierf, M.
abstract: Force spectroscopy enables direct investigation of the interplay between free energy and transition kinetics in proteins and nucleic acids. However, multi-domain proteins often display multiple intermediate structures with diverse stabilities and kinetics, making equilibrium conditions difficult to achieve and out-of-equilibrium experiments challenging to interpret. We introduce a single-molecule force spectroscopy assay using periodic forces and high-resolution magnetic tweezers to bridge different stabilities, selectively enhance intermediate populations, and rigorously analyze multi-domain protein folding kinetics at quasi-equilibrium. By applying well-defined periodic square force functions with tunable steady states, we first validate our framework on the two-state folder {lambda}6-85, demonstrating that periodic force experiments can reproduce equilibrium kinetics. Extending this approach to the multi-domain protein mimic (Protein L), we show that tuning force, frequency, and amplitude enhances populations of distinct intermediate states. Finally, we dissect the entangled states of the hybrid two-domain protein {lambda}-L, where a 100-fold difference in domain kinetics precludes equilibrium analysis, by expanding from a two-state to a three-state periodic force protocol to direct intermediate populations. Our assay and analysis framework open new possibilities for deciphering complex multi-domain folds and their multi-dimensional folding pathways.

title: Pathogenic DRP1 variants reveal a role for biomolecular condensation in mitochondrial fission
authors: Ross, K. A.; Travis, A. M.; Harwig, M. C.; Young, M. S.; Rodas Montejo, E. H.; Farah, M. J.; Donohue, M. J.; Taylor, R. W.; Olahova, M.; Hill, R. B.
abstract: Fission is essential for proper mitochondrial function and for cellular homeostasis. Dysfunction in mitochondrial fission is associated with several neurological disorders, including the rare and lethal encephalopathy EMPF1, which is caused by de novo heterozygous DNM1L variants. DNM1L encodes the mitochondrial fission mechanoenzyme DRP1, which can intrinsically self-assemble and induce membrane scission. Wild-type DRP1 puncta that appear throughout the cytoplasm are thought to be pre-scission complexes of well-ordered oligomeric assemblies. Immunofluorescence imaging of patient-derived EMPF1 fibroblasts carrying assembly-deficient DNM1L variants reveals elongated mitochondrial networks consistent with impaired fission. Despite this loss-of-function phenotype, these cells retain essentially wild-type numbers of DRP1 puncta. We confirmed the previously reported inability of purified pathogenic DRP1 variants p.Gly363Asp and p.Gly401Ser to assemble under conditions in which WT DRP1 forms helical polymers. Under macromolecular crowding conditions, however, both wild-type and mutant DRP1 access condensed states whose formation depends on protein concentration and solution conditions. Acute treatment of EMPF1 fibroblasts with 1,6-hexanediol preferentially alters DRP1 puncta fluorescence intensity and distribution in mutant cells relative to wild type, indicating genotype-dependent differences in puncta material properties. Together, these findings support a model in which DRP1 puncta occupy a continuum of condensed states, only a subset of which mature into fission-competent assemblies, revealing biomolecular condensation as a previously unrecognized layer of DRP1 regulation. Biasing DRP1 along this continuum may provide a mechanistic basis for impaired fission in EMPF1 and suggest opportunities to restore productive assembly in select pathogenic contexts.
